name: Slovak
confidence_why: Every source read puts Slovak main stress fixed on the first syllable of the word (Sabol 1986, Sabol & Zimmermann 1994, Kráľ 1984, Horák 1985, Benuš & Mády 2010, Mocová 2012, Dogil 1995 via StressTyp2); the sources differ only over secondary stress, which Sabol 1986 denies as a systemic feature while Kráľ 1984 places it on the third or penultimate syllable of longer words and Dogil's survey on alternating odd syllables, so the alternating pattern in the record's rule string is the one part not backed by the native literature.
catalog_quote: The stress rule operates on prosodic words as a whole, so affixes are stress-sensitive.
sweep_summary: Slovak (slov1269) is in the catalog as fixed-strict initial stress with an alternating secondary profile, the deciding text being an StressTyp2 paraphrase of Dogil (1999) rather than a quotation. this search of works with stress in the title produced one bibliography item: Sabol, J. 1981, 'The Prosodic Structure of the Slovak Word', Prague Studies in Mathematical Linguistics 7 (LLSEE 9), pp. 59-80, John Benjamins, doi:10.1075/llsee.9.05sab. It is relevant (word stress of Slovak, by the principal Slovak prosodist) but closed: Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar both report no open copy and no abstract; Benjamins (an automated-access block block) and De Gruyter (empty response) are could not be reached by automated download; HathiTrust has no record for either ISBN; archive.org holds only vol. 1 (1966); Open Library shows no ebook; Records (, blocked landing pages, HathiTrust/Google Books responses) and. Priority for acquisition: medium — an English-language first-hand statement, but the same author's fuller stress article (Sabol 1986, SAS 15:391-412) is already held by the project and was re-read: it states fixed first-syllable stress (p. 392), prosodic-word domain with stressed monosyllabic prepositions (p. 405), and denies systemic secondary stress (pp. 395-396, citing Petreková 1986), while quoting Kráľ 1984:164's orthoepic 3rd/penult secondary stress. That held statement confirms the catalog's initial primary stress and word domain and contradicts its 101/10101 secondary profile; it supersedes the StressTyp2/Dogil paraphrase as the deciding source. all findings come from DOI/API records and pages actually opened.

new_statements.quote: Prízvuk je v spisovnej slovenčine fixný, viazaný na prvú slabiku slova (Zajtra pôjdeme domov). Viazanosť prízvuku v slovenčine vylučuje jeho schopnosť rozlišovať význam (na rozdiel od jazykov s voľným prízvukom, napríklad ruštiny). Fixné miesto prízvuku na 1. slabike slova a tvaru rozhodujúcim spôsobom určuje prozodický charakter spisovnej slovenčiny [...] Experimentálny prieskum intenzity kriviek pri analýze slovenského prízvuku (Petreková, 1986) však ukazuje, že tzv. vedľajší prízvuk v spisovnej slovenčine neexistuje ako systémový jav.
new_statements.translation: Stress in standard Slovak is fixed, bound to the first syllable of the word (Zajtra pôjdeme domov 'Tomorrow we go home'). The boundness of stress in Slovak excludes its ability to distinguish meaning (unlike languages with free stress, e.g. Russian). The fixed place of stress on the 1st syllable of the word and word-form decisively determines the prosodic character of standard Slovak [...] Experimental examination of intensity curves in the analysis of Slovak stress (Petreková 1986), however, shows that so-called secondary stress does not exist in standard Slovak as a systemic phenomenon.
new_statements.citation: Sabol, Ján. 1986. Prízvuk v slovenčine. In J. Mistrík (ed.), Studia Academica Slovaca 15, 391-412. Bratislava: Alfa.
new_statements.locator: p. 392, sect. 1.0 (the text); secondary stress p. 395-396, sect. 2.1 (the text)
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by the leading Slovak phonetician: primary stress is fixed on the first syllable of the (prosodic) word, non-contrastive; monosyllabic prepositions normally take the stress (sect. 3.3.1, p. 405), so the domain is the prosodic word, matching the catalog's word domain and 'fixed-strict' initial coding. On secondary stress Sabol explicitly rejects any systemic secondary stress (ratio 1 : n-1), while quoting the orthoepic codification (Kráľ 1984:164) that places a weaker secondary stress on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words and the 3rd or penultimate of longer words. Neither position yields the catalog's alternating-with-final profile (101, 10101..). This is the same reading the 2026-09-16 check reached; this search of works with stress in the title adds nothing new because the one target (Sabol 1981) is closed.

tone_statements.translation: In Standard Slovak, stress is bound to the first syllable of the word (Zajtra pôjdeme domov.). The boundness of stress in Standard Slovak excludes its ability to distinguish meaning (unlike languages with free stress, e.g. Russian). [...] Tonal modulation is the term for changes in the height of the fundamental tone (pitch) of speech. Tonal modulation of the articulatory stream gives rise to further suprasegmental phenomena: voice register and melody. [...] The melody of the sentence is connected with the conceptual and emotional content of the sentence.

audit.recode_to: Primary-initial fixed stays. Secondary profile: drop the alternating '+final' odd-syllable pattern (alternating stress from the left). Default reclassify as initial-only initial stress following Sabol 1986:395-396 and Sabol & Zimmermann 1994 (secondary stress 'neexistuje ako systemovy jav'; ratio 1:n-1), with a caution note carrying the orthoepic alternative from Kral 1984:164 (4-syl 1010; 5+ third-or-penult, e.g. 10100~10010) as a register-dependent variant. Under no Slovak source seen is a trisyllable 101 or a final syllable secondary-stressed, so at minimum n=3,5,7 must change.

sources.note: Suprasegmentals presented after Sabol by temporal / force / tonal modulation. Stress: bound to the first syllable, therefore unable to distinguish meaning (contrast drawn with free-stress Russian), delimitative; one-syllable prepositions usually stressed. 'Tonal modulation' = changes of F0, producing only voice register and sentence melody (melodéma on the nuclear stretch decides sentence modality; cadence types follow). No lexical tone or pitch accent; pitch is intonational.

sources.citation: Sabol, Ján. 1977. Prozodický systém slovenčiny a slovenský verš. In Jozef Mistrík (ed.), Studia Academica Slovaca 6: Prednášky XIII. letného seminára slovenského jazyka a kultúry, 491-515. Bratislava: Alfa.
sources.note: Sect. 1.0-1.1 (pp. 493-495) set out the Slovak prosodic system before turning to verse: word-level phonological devices are quantity (temporal modulation) and stress (force modulation), syllabification and word boundary; melody, pause and emphasis are sentence-level intonational devices with a grammaticalizing function. Slovak 'confirms the incompatibility of free quantity and free stress': quantity is distinctive, stress has 'only' a phonological-delimitative function (fixed, marks word/measure boundaries). No lexical use of pitch.
